He propped himself up on the frame and climbed along the corner of the building, reaching the top in a moment. He walked briskly across the roof. He went back and forth three or four times, and then suddenly leaped down, standing straight. The Prince had a favored concubine who was skilled at the *pipa* <gloss>Chinese lute</gloss>. The *pipa* she played was made with warm jade tuning pegs. Embracing it, the room felt warm. The concubine treasured it, and it was not shown to anyone unless ordered by the Prince. One evening, there was a banquet, and a guest asked to see its wonder. The Prince, however, was lazy and promised it for the following day. Baozhu was standing to the side and said, "Without the Prince's order, I can still retrieve it." The Prince had people ride to inform the residence to be on guard, and only then sent him. Baozhu scaled over a dozen high walls to reach the concubine's courtyard. He saw lights in the room, but the doors were locked and he could not enter. Under the corridor, there was a parrot sleeping on a stand. Baozhu imitated the sound of a cat. Then he imitated the parrot's call, shouting urgently, "A cat is coming!" while flapping and making sounds as if it were being attacked. *A. AURICOMUS*, smaller, thinner, with a yellowish pileus, striate margin, a fistulose stipe, and affixed, ventricose, whitish-brown lamellae. *Batsch. f. 21.* On burned ground, to be separated from the yellowish-stemmed *A. geophyllus*, strikingly rimose.

701. *A. PERBREVIS*, with a subfleshy, convex, obtusely umbonate, longitudinally fibrous or squamose pileus, with a substriate margin, finally fissured, a stuffed, short, pale, white-fibrillose stipe, slightly attenuated at the base, and uncinate-adnexed, subdistant, whitish-brownish or argillaceous lamellae. *Weinm. p. 185. A. ereus. Secr. n. 304.* In broad-leaved woods, rare. Small, but rather firm, brownish or reddish-yellow, stipe barely an inch, cortinate, opaque, pruinose at the apex. Flesh white.

702. *A. HIULCUS*, with a subfleshy, conical-expanded, umbonate, fibrillose, rimose-squamose pileus, a stuffed, rigid, elongated, silky-fibrillose stipe, white-pruinose at the apex and white-fleshed, and subfree, barely crowded, broad, white-fleshed lamellae, darker at the base, finally olivaceous. *Batt. t. 18. C.!* — *A. lacerus Secr. n. 318, 319* also seem to be here. On pine forest ground. Odor, to me, abounding in sneezing powder, obsolete. Stipe 2—3 inches long, 2 lines thick, slightly curved, equal, with a bulbillose base. Pileus brown, olive.

703. *A. GRATUS*, with a subfleshy, conical-campanulate, fibrillose pileus, expanded, rimose, umbonate, with a darker squamose disc, a stuffed, shiny, fibrillose, flexuous, white-reddish stipe, and adnexed, crowded, thin, olive-pale to brownish lamellae. *Weinm.! p. 185. — Secr. n. 311*, who leads *Bull. t. 522. f. 2* here not without veracity of the species. In grassy places. It approaches *A. geophyllus* or *A. scabellus* rather closely, easily distinct by its pleasant anise odor. Pileus whitish or yellowish-reddish. Stipe obsoletely pruinose at the apex. (v. s.)

704. *A. TRINII*, with a subfleshy, hemispherical, obtuse, longitudinally reddish-fibrillose pileus, a stuffed, equal, slender, loosely red-fibrillose, white-farinaceous stipe, and rounded, ventricose, cinnamon lamellae, white-flocculose at the edge. *Weinm.! p. 194.* In grassy broad-leaved woods. At Saint Petersburg! Rare, significant, heteroclitic! with a carnation odor. Pileus barely rimose, nor squamose, ½ inch, whitish-reddish, tawny when dry.

Day. "Beautiful, it is indeed beautiful, but it is not yet great." Yao asked: "Then how should it be?" Shun said:
<margin>Originally without contrived action to bring about governance, and the myriad things are naturally peaceful. Therefore</margin>
<margin>Sentence structure</margin>
Heaven’s Virtue brings forth peace. The sun and moon shine, and the four seasons proceed. It is like the sun and moon having
<margin>The appearance of movement and chaos</margin>
their cycles. The clouds move and the rain is bestowed. Yao said: "Then is it all stirred up and restless?" The Son
is the union of Heaven. I am the union of humanity. As for Heaven and Earth, they are what the ancients considered great,
and what the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun collectively praised. Therefore, those of the past who ruled the world,
what did they do? They simply followed Heaven and Earth.

# הלכות אונאה ומקח טעות
## שחלקו וטעות ובו לט סעיפים

<margin>סימן רכו (א) מלילה לכל למנא היתר לחפש כלים וסחורות נגד התובעים להטמיט מהן כלל טודקי כדי שיתרצו לפסר"ס ט"ו וסרמ"ד ועכ"פ סוחפים טעמו סחורה עם ישראל אחר ונסתלקו מן העכ"ס מס"ז הכל מן הישראל אבל אם כדייכם יכול להסתלק מן העכ"ס ואין להם שום טענה על הישראל מסלס חלקו וכן ל"מ וסלמ"ס כ"ט פ"ה סי' מ"ח (ג) והם סלס" מצע משומין מהמוכר ומח"כ הזר בו ורוצה לקיים המקח מחלוקת בין המחור הגדול ומלמח"כ פ' נפרק הספינה (ד) כתב סמ"ע וסס ככ' מקום ל"ס ססס"י סס"י ל"ט לחין כפי' נ' הלכת' כינכו חליכת דכ"ט דהא ליכא טעות דסוס סל ולמה זה יחלוק עליו מורס לכל כסנס למזוב דין המרדכי כתב כנגד כ"ה (ו) ובית חדס פסק סיכול לחזור זו ממינו חזר אין לכדי' סירלה למגר מו לקרותו (ל) ולמ"ר סיס מונחה לקרקעי ל' לכ"ח ל"ט לולס חזור ססרו בקק"מ תמיד נמקומו ועין בחורד ל' לכ"ח ל"ט כוס כלל כ' וכ"ס סימן כ"ט ועי"א דף ט"פ (ו) כתב</margin>

רכו עד כמה הוה מחילה או חזרת האונאה ושליח שטעוה ואחים

א. חסור להונות את חבירו בין במקחו (א) בין בממכרו ואיזה מהם שחינה בין לוקח בין מוכר עובר בלאו: ב. כמה תהיה ההונאה ויהיה חייב להשיב מתיא כטוב עוד הרי שמכר שוה סס בחמש לו טוף שש בט סה חמש בטס לו מתיא סס כטטט הרי זה הונאה וקנה המקח וחייב המוכר סוה טבעס בטסיס למתנה: ג. היתה ההונאה פחות מזה בכל שהו סמכר סוה טבעס בטסיס ופרוטה חייב להחזיר כלום שכל פחות משתות דרך הכל למחול כו: ד. היתה ההונאה יתרה על השתות כל שהו מכר סוה ס' לחמש פחות סו סתק יתר מן השיעור שיתבטל המקח ויוכל לחזור בו וכן קלכס הממכר הרי יכול לחזור (ב) חס רנה זה לקבל נסמוך סעיף ז' (טור ססס הר"י וסר"מ) מוכר לו סוה ס' לח לפסד דליכא כהן הונאה שאין לו דטעי חייבי: (ד) דטעי חייבי: (ה) הרי טעות היתר על פרוטה היתה פרוטה כטוב מית חבירו בפחות משתות חס יט בונחה הר"מ וסר"מ (ו) יש להתפקק לס מותר הניע לכדי' מותר לכתחלה להשיב מתיא כטוב ניפה: ו. עד מתי יכול לחזור ולתבוע השתות ודבטס המקח ביותר משתות עד שיראה לתגר או לקרובו וכל שהו יותר מיכו יכול לחזור ולתבוע הונחתו וחס יברר שזה לו מוכס ועל כן לחקור כתוך זמן זה לידע חס נתנה יכול לחזור ונתבע שהרי מחול: ט. כמה דברים חמורים בטסלס ססמכת וסומק (ז) ימיל חזר הלקוחה קודם זה סירלה:

# Choshen Mishpat: Laws of Overcharging and Invalid Sales 226

## Overcharging and Mistake, with 30 sections

226: How much is forgiveness or returning the overcharge, and an agent who made a mistake, and others

1. It is forbidden to overcharge one's neighbor, whether in his purchase or in his sale, and whoever does so—whether buyer or seller—transgresses a negative commandment.

2. How much must the overcharge be for [one] to be obligated to return the money? If he sold [an item] worth six for five, or worth five for six, this is an overcharge, and the purchase stands, and the seller is obligated to return the overcharge to the buyer.

3. If the overcharge was less than this, even a little bit—if he sold worth six for six and a *perutah*—he is not obligated to return anything, for everything less than a sixth is considered forgiven.

4. If the overcharge was more than a sixth, even a little bit—[e.g.,] he sold worth six for five, less a *perutah*—the sale is void, and one can retract it; and similarly, in [every] sale, one can retract if one [party] wishes to accept [the loss].

5. If one sold worth six for five—and there is no overcharge, for there are no "deceivers" [in this case]—...if the overcharge was more than a *perutah*, he must return it; [if] it was a *perutah*, he must return it to his neighbor; if it is less than a sixth, if [the seller] forgives... [the Sages] say: it is permitted for a person to return the money [if he chooses to].

6. Until when can one return and claim the sixth and [cancel] the sale? Until he shows it to a merchant or his relative. And for any [amount] more than that, he can return and claim his overcharge. And if he clarifies that this [item] is known to him, he can investigate within this time [to know] if he was deceived, [and if] he can return and claim, for he [has already] forgiven [it].

7. [Regarding] several serious things, if he returns [the item]...

<column-break/>

10. If he knows about the overcharge, if he leaves the purchase in his hand and he [continues] to use it, the seller has retracted [his claim].
[Regarding] several serious things, if the buyer says: "The purchase is in my hand and I will use it," the seller has retracted [his claim].

11. There is no need to say regarding the cancellation of a purchase, where he does not know the value [of the item] until he shows it to a merchant. Therefore, if the purchase was an item that does not change [in value], such as pepper and similar [things], if he did not claim it, he cannot return and claim, for he has forgiven [it].

12. If he sold because of his distress and he sold it for less than the value [of] the mistake, [because] he sold [it] due to distress, he cannot return [it] and [the buyer] is forgiven.

13. [If] he sold worth four for five, the sale is void, and he did not manage to show it to a merchant or his relative, and now [the value] stands at the buyer's price, he can retract it, [but] the seller cannot [claim] "I have profited," [if] he has not [yet] realized the profit.

14. Similarly, [if] a seller [sold] worth five for four, and it stands at the buyer's price, the seller can retract [the sale], and the buyer cannot say to the seller: "Not because of me [the price] changed," [for he can] retract [the sale] if he has not [yet] realized the profit.

15. [If] he sold worth five for six, and he did not manage to show it until it increased and stood at [its new] price, the seller is obligated to return [it], and [he is] obligated to return [it] if it increased in the buyer's domain.

16. Similarly, if he sold six for five, and the price dropped to four, the buyer is obligated to return [the difference] to the seller, for the sale was acquired and [it] dropped in the buyer's domain.

Omni prenitida compositis corpore forma:
Nomen Pelagius, formæ splendore decorus.
Consilio prudens, tota bonitate refulgens.
Qui vix transactis iam tunc puerilibus annis.
Attigit ætatis primos flores iuuenilis.
Cumque fat inimitem patri sciret fore regem:
Tali merentem blandis voce parentem.
Mi chare pater mea suscipe verba libenter.
Et que commoneo sensu bene pcipe prompto.
Calleo namque tuam senio decrescere vitam,
Viribus et propriis neruos penitus vacuos:
Nec te posse quidem leuis quid ferre laboris.
Ast ego sed validis dominabor quippe lacertis:
Ad tempusque potens dominis succubere duris.
Quapropter moneo: precibus blandisque rogabo:
Vt tregi natum me deponas tibi charum.
Donec sufficias precium persoluere totum.
Ne tua canicies vinclis intercidat artis.
Tsenior contra dicebat voce seuera.
Define tanta loqui dulcissime define fili.
Ne merore meos ducas in tartara canos.
Nonne salute tua pendet tantum mea vita,
Et sine te spaciu valeo pie viuere nullum.
Te decus omne meu, tu gloria magna parentu.
Es quoque subiecti nobis spes sola popelli.
Quapropter patria prestat me linquere charam.
Ecnon hyspania uinctu penetrare superbam.
Qua te grandeue vinclis spem tradere vitæ.
On tulit ergo patre Pelagius ista sequente.
Sed mulcet dictis mente chari genitoris.
Et cogit blandis quod suasit velle loquelis.
Consenfit precibus tandem genitor venerandus:
Tradidit et natum, semet redimedo misellum.
Tunc rex Pelagiu iussit perducere secum.
Et lætus rediit patria victorque reuisit.
Vllus pro meritis credat factu fore regis:
Hoc quod tam pulcra uincebat denique pompa.
Sed mage iudicio secreto iudicis æqui.
Vt populus tanto correptus rite flagello:
Fleret tocius proprii comissa reatus.
Vel que Pelagius christi pro lege necandus:
Forte locum peteret quo se morti dare posset.
Ecnon sanguineu pro christo fundere riuu.
Impendens anima domino bene morte piata.

<header>OF PELAGIUS.</header>

With every shape of his body composed in beauty,
By name Pelagius, decorated with the splendor of his form,
Prudent in counsel, shining in all goodness,
Who, having scarcely passed his childish years,
Reached the first flowers of his youthful age.
And when he knew the king to be an enemy to his father,
He addressed his deserving parent with such flattering voice:
My dear father, receive my words willingly,
And what I advise, take in well with ready sense.
I am aware that your life is decreasing with age,
And your nerves are deeply empty of their own strength,
And that you cannot indeed bear any of the light labor.
But I shall indeed rule with strong arms,
And for a time be able to submit to the harsh masters.
Wherefore I advise: I will ask with prayers and flatteries,
That you hand me, your dear son, over to the king,
Until you have enough to pay the full price,
Lest your gray hairs perish in the bonds of art.
The elder, on the contrary, spoke with a severe voice:
Cease to speak such things, cease, my sweetest son,
Lest you lead my gray hairs into the underworld with sorrow.
Does not my life depend so much on your safety,
And without you, I am able to live no space of time peacefully.
You are my whole honor, you are the great glory of your parents,
You are also the only hope of the people subject to us.
Wherefore it is better to leave me behind than the dear fatherland,
And also to penetrate proud Hispania in bonds,
Where I might trade your life, the hope of my age, for chains.
Pelagius did not take this, therefore, as his father followed,
But he soothes the mind of his dear parent with words,
And compels him with flattering speeches to want what he advised.
The venerable father finally consented to the prayers:
And handed over his son, redeeming himself, the miserable one.
Then the king ordered Pelagius to be led with him,
And he returned happy, and revisited his fatherland as a victor.
Let no one believe this happened for the merits of the king,
That which he conquered with such beautiful pomp,
But rather by the secret judgment of the just Judge,
So that the people, corrected rightly by such a lash,
Might weep for the committed guilt of all their own,
Or that Pelagius, to be killed for the law of Christ,
Might by chance seek the place where he could give himself to death,
And also shed the bloody stream for Christ,
Wasting his soul to the Lord, well-atoned by death.

ausgaben aber fällt an die Familie des Stifters. Es ist klar, daß in dieser letzteren Bestimmung der eigentliche Zweck der Stiftung liegt: in der Form der Klostergründung, in Wahrheit ein sakral geschütztes, insbesondere, als Klostergut, gegen den Zugriff der weltlichen — und das hieß der patrimonial-bürokratischen — Gewalten geschütztes Familienfideikommiß mit voraussichtlich steigenden Einkünften. (Nebenher erreicht der Stifter noch den Zweck, das Wohlgefallen Gottes und der Menschen zu erringen und, unter Umständen, seiner Familie Einfluß auf die Besetzung der Mönchspründen und also Gelegenheit zu Gefälligkeiten an einflußreiche Familien — denn die Mönchspräbenden waren oft tatsächlich so gut wie pflichtlose Sinekuren für Konstantinopeler Garçons, da nicht nur Klausur, sondern auch Residenzpflicht fehlte — und auch Einfluß auf die Art der Verwaltung einer Familienkapelle zu sichern). Das ganze war eine Art von geldwirtschaftlichem Surrogat für das „Eigenkirchenwesen“ des feudalen Okzidents. Es scheint, daß Stiftungen in ganz ähnlicher Form schon unter der altägyptischen Patrimonialherrschaft vorkommen. Genau die gleiche Erscheinung findet sich jedenfalls im mittelalterlichen Islam als „Wakuf“ (Stiftung für Moscheen u. dgl.) wieder, wie es die Urkunden bezeugen. Und zwar wurden auch damals gerade Objekte, welche Geldwert, und zwar steigenden, tragen: Baugrund, Ergasterien (vermietbare Werkstätten) gestiftet, ganz ohne Zweifel zu dem gleichen Zweck und aus dem gleichen Grunde: weil die Weihe zum Kirchengut, wenn auch keine absolute Sicherheit, so doch das Optimum von Garantie gegen die willkürlichen Eingriffe der weltlichen Beamtenschaft bot. So wirkt die Willkür und Unberechenbarkeit der patrimonialen Herrschaft ihrerseits dahin, das Gebiet sakralrechtlicher Gebundenheit zu verstärken. Und da andererseits die theoretische Starrheit und Unabänderlichkeit der Scharî'a in ihrer subjektiven und oft ganz unberechenbaren Interpretation durch die Richter ihre „Korrektur“ fand, so steigerten sich die beiden der Entwicklung des Kapitalismus gleich feindlichen Bestandteile des Patrimonialismus gegenseitig. Denn daß die höchst nachhaltige Immobilisierung akkumulierten Besitzes in Gestalt der Wakufgebundenheit — ganz dem Geist der antiken Wirtschaft entsprechend, welche akkumuliertes Vermögen als Rentenfonds, nicht als Erwerbskapital benutzte — für die ökonomische Entwicklung des Orients von sehr großer Bedeutung gewesen ist, nimmt C. H. Becker sicher mit Recht an. (Durch spanische Vermittlung ist dann das, wahrscheinlich eine säkularisierte Nachbildung des Wakuf bildende, Institut des profanen „Fideikommisses“, welches dort zuerst auftaucht, im 17. Jahrhundert nach Deutschland importiert worden.) —

Und endlich war dem Patrimonialismus gerade auf dem Boden einer relativ entwickelten Geldwirtschaft und speziell in Epochen, wo er sich einem rationalen bürokratischen System stark annähert, noch eine Art der Einwirkung auf die ökonomische Entwicklung eigen, die aus der Form seiner Bedarfsdeckung folgte. Wie der „Patrimonialstaat“ sich leicht in ein Bündel von Privilegien auflöste, so lag ihm auch einerseits die monopolistisch-erwerbswirtschaftliche, andererseits die privilegierende Bedarfsdeckung (im früher besprochenen Sinn des Wortes) besonders nahe. Mit Hilfe eines gut funktionierenden Patrimonialbeamtentums ließen sich alle Arten fiskalischer Unternehmungen und Monopole besonders leicht durchführen. Sowohl der ägyptische wie der spätrömische Staat und die Staaten des nahen und fernen Ostens haben in teilweise sehr umfassender Weise Staatsbetriebe geschaffen und auch Monopole ausnutzt, und die Regiegewerbe von Fürsten der beginnenden Neuzeit liegen in dieser Richtung. Die erwerbswirtschaftliche öffentliche Bedarfsdeckung ist keineswegs auf den Patrimonialismus beschränkt geblieben: auch die Kommunen haben im Mittelalter und im Beginn der Neuzeit sich, oft mit großen Verlusten (so Frankfurt a. M.), auch an recht gewagten gewerblichen oder Handelsunternehmungen von reinem Erwerbscharakter beteiligt. Aber der Wirkungsradius von Monopolen für die öffentliche Erwerbswirtschaft war bei Patrimonialstaaten, allgemein gesprochen, naturgemäß größer und daher die öffentlichen Monopole

It is clear that the actual purpose of the foundation lies in this latter provision: it is, in the form of a monastery founding, in truth a family trust <term>Familienfideikommiß</term> <gloss>entail</gloss> protected in a sacred manner, specifically protected as monastery property against the seizure of worldly—and that meant patrimonial-bureaucratic—powers, with presumably increasing income. (Incidentally, the founder also achieves the goal of gaining the pleasure of God and men and, under certain circumstances, of securing for his family influence on the occupation of the monastic prebends and thus the opportunity for favors to influential families—for the monastic prebends were often in fact as good as duty-free sinecures for Constantinople's bachelors, since not only cloister life but also the obligation of residence was missing—and also influence on the manner of the administration of a family chapel). The whole thing was a kind of money-economic substitute for the "proprietary church system" <term>Eigenkirchenwesen</term> <gloss>system where a landlord owns the church on his land</gloss> of the feudal Occident. It seems that foundations in a very similar form already occurred under ancient Egyptian patrimonial rule. Exactly the same phenomenon is found in any case in the medieval Islam as "Wakuf" (foundation for mosques and the like) again, as the documents testify. And indeed, even then, objects that carry monetary value, and specifically increasing value, were endowed: construction land, <term>ergasteria</term> <gloss>rentable workshops</gloss>, without a doubt for the same purpose and for the same reason: because the consecration as church property, even if it offered no absolute security, nonetheless offered the optimum of guarantee against the arbitrary interventions of the worldly bureaucracy. Thus, the arbitrariness and unpredictability of patrimonial rule acts in its turn to strengthen the area of sacred-legal boundedness. And since, on the other hand, the theoretical rigidity and immutability of the <term>Scharî'a</term> <gloss>Islamic religious law</gloss> found its "correction" in its subjective and often quite unpredictable interpretation by the judges, the two components of patrimonialism that are equally hostile to the development of capitalism mutually intensified one another. For C. H. Becker is certainly correct in assuming that the highly lasting immobilization of accumulated property in the form of Wakuf-binding—entirely in accordance with the spirit of the ancient economy, which used accumulated wealth as a rent fund, not as acquisition capital—has been of very great importance for the economic development of the Orient. (Through Spanish mediation, the institution of the profane "entail," which likely forms a secularized imitation of the Wakuf and which first appears there, was then imported into Germany in the 17th century.) —

And finally, patrimonialism, precisely on the soil of a relatively developed money economy and especially in epochs where it strongly approaches a rational bureaucratic system, possessed yet another type of influence on economic development, which followed from the form of its supply fulfillment. Just as the "patrimonial state" easily dissolved into a bundle of privileges, so too was it particularly inclined, on the one hand, to monopolistic-acquisitive and, on the other, to preferential supply fulfillment (in the sense of the word discussed earlier). With the help of a well-functioning patrimonial civil service, all kinds of fiscal enterprises and monopolies could be carried out particularly easily. Both the Egyptian and the late Roman state, as well as the states of the Near and Far East, created state-run enterprises in a partially very comprehensive manner and also utilized monopolies, and the state-run businesses of princes of the early modern period lie in this direction. Acquisitive public supply fulfillment has by no means remained limited to patrimonialism: the communes in the Middle Ages and the beginning of the modern era also participated, often with large losses (such as Frankfurt am Main), in quite daring industrial or commercial enterprises of a purely acquisitive character. <header>THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI</header>

1. Since the papyrus must on palaeographical grounds be assigned to the end of the first or the early part of the second century, the coincidence of a 6th intercalary day with the 10th year of an emperor called Germanicus fixes the reign as that of either Domitian or Trajan. The supplement at the end of l. 1 is in any case long compared with the 10 letters which are missing in l. 2, and Domitian is therefore preferable.

6. Cf. the similar beginning of <term>P. Edmondst.</term> 6 sqq. For "Zeus, Earth, and Sun", cf. 48. 6, &c.

12. "In the street" is supplied from the newly found emancipation (cf. introd.); cf. "in the same street" in ll. 34-5. We are inclined to think that this formula, which so far is only known at Oxyrhynchus, regularly implies the execution of the document before the <term>agoranomi</term> <gloss>market-inspectors</gloss>, who are mentioned much less frequently in Oxyrhynchus contracts than elsewhere.

16-9. The newly found emancipation proceeds straight from the description of the slave to the mention of the <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss> corresponding to l. 19, and owing to the lacunae it is not clear whether the sum mentioned in l. 17 is the ransom of the whole slave or of the 2/3 previously set free. On the whole we think the latter hypothesis is more likely. The talents are in either case probably copper.

19. <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss>: the newly found emancipation has "coined silver drachmae ten and what is assigned for her... to Theon (the owner)... ransom 500 silver drachmae," on the analogy of which we have supplied "ransom" in l. 24. It is clear from that papyrus that a distinction was drawn between the payment in <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss> and the ransom paid to the owner, and from 48 and 49 in which the same amount of <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss>, 10 drachmae, is coupled with different sums expressed in copper, there would seem to have been a normal charge of 10 drachmae in addition to the ransom, in spite of 722. 19-20, where the amount of <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss> cannot be 10 drachmae. The divergence of 722 at this point may be due to the fact that it is concerned with the emancipation of only part of a slave. To whom these 10 drachmae were paid is not made clear, but it is probable that the State in some form was the recipient. Nowhere in connexion with these emancipations under Graeco-Egyptian law is there a mention of the <term>vicesima libertatis</term> <gloss>tax on manumission</gloss> levied under Roman law, which appears in <term>B. G. U.</term> 96. 8 (the customary twentieth); but if, as we are now disposed to think, the status of the persons who wrote 48-9 stand towards such documents as 722 in the same kind of relation as 241-3 towards contracts for sale or mortgage, there must have been a tax upon the emancipation of slaves apart from the 10 drachmae <term>argyriou episemou</term> <gloss>coined silver</gloss>.

**PAPYRUS EDMONDSTONE.** A.D. 354.

...Under the consulship of our masters Constantius Augustus for the 7th time and Constantius the most noble Caesar for the 3rd time.
Tubi 17, 18th indiction, in the city of Elephantine of the upper Thebaid.
Aurelia Teroutirou daughter of Pasmes, her mother being Tsenpachnoumis, from the city of Elephantine, with the presence of her lawful husband Aurelius Dorotheus son of Serenus from the same city, to Aurelius Sarapammon son of Tapamon and Tkaletis, whose mother is Thaesis, and to her daughter Aurelia Lousia, who have been slaves to me, as regards the portion falling to me, greeting. I agree voluntarily, of my own free will, and irrevocably to set you free as regards the portion falling to me, under Earth and Heaven, in accordance with the piety of the all-merciful God, having come to me by inheritance from my mother, from now and for all time.

The husband <note>referring to Wutou</note> and the others, hearing this, bowed and looked at her; only then were they comforted. Shortly after, they stopped to arrange the tomb of the Mu family, and only then was she buried together with them.

Strange indeed. The woman knew the gratitude of being understood <note>original: "zhi ji" <gloss>having one's worth recognized</gloss></note> and dedicated her life to him; this is something even a heroic man would find difficult. What did that woman know, yet she was as magnificent and extraordinary as this? If one were to meet <term>Jiufang Gao</term> <gloss>a legendary expert in judging horses</gloss>, he would certainly see her as a thoroughbred.

How beautiful the character of Qiao Niang is; her virtue is truly complete. She did not serve two husbands, which is chastity. She sought to repay the one who understood her, which is righteousness. She stepped forward to confront the officials, which is courage. She cried and pleaded with shrinking humility, which is wisdom. She endured poverty without being tainted, which is integrity. She raised the child from infancy and taught him as he grew, which is benevolence and propriety. Even after her death, she was still able to stop her coffin and rebuke her son, eventually succeeding in her wish to be buried in her original home. She was a perfected person in the underworld. Alas, how miraculous!

If a co-heir has purchased land from a creditor.
17. MODESTINUS, Book 9, Rules.
He who has co-heirs, if he has purchased from a creditor <note>original: "(1)"</note> land given as a pledge by his testator, ought not to be summoned by the co-heirs in an action for the division of common property.

Concerning the imposition of a servitude, and the power of the judge.
18. JAVOLENUS, Book 2, Epistles.
An arbiter cannot arrange for hereditary land to serve non-hereditary land <note>original: "(2)"</note>: because the power of the judge cannot exceed that which has been brought into judgment <note>original: "(3)"</note>.
Concerning those things which are on the boundary. 1. Concerning the vestibule. 2. Concerning the road, and the expenses made upon it. 3. Concerning a slave who is in flight. 4. Concerning an aqueduct.
19. PAULUS, Book 6, on Sabinus.
A tree which has grown on the boundary <note>original: "(4)"</note>, likewise a stone which extends through both pieces of land, as long as it adheres to the land, are the property of both parties from the region of their respective boundaries: nor do they come into the action for the division of common property: but when either the stone has been removed, or the tree uprooted or cut down, it shall become common undivided property: and it will come into the action for the division of common property: for that which was in defined parts is again confounded. Wherefore, two masses of two owners having been melted together, the whole mass is common <note>original: "(5)"</note>, even if something from the first form remains separated: thus, a tree and a stone separated from the land confound the right of ownership.
§. 1. An arbiter for the division of common property ought not to be given for a common vestibule <note>original: "(6)"</note> <note>original: "(7)"</note> of two buildings if either party is unwilling: because he who is compelled to bid <note>original: "(8)"</note> for the vestibule necessarily has to set a price for the whole of the buildings at times, if he has no other access <note>original: "(9)"</note>.
§. 2. If a road is owed to us through the same place, and expense has been made upon it, Pomponius says that it is more difficult for an action for the division of common property or an action on partnership to be brought: For what community of right <note>original: "(10)"</note> can be understood separately? But an action for the management of another's affairs <note>original: "(11)"</note> should be brought.

<column-break/>

§. 3. The judge in an action for the division of common property, as also in the action for the division of an inheritance, ought to order those among whom he is the judge to bid for a slave who is in flight <note>original: "(12)"</note>: and then adjudicate him to the one with whom the bidding remained: and there will be no danger that, by decree of the Senate, the penalty of the Fabian law be committed.
§. 4. Labeo says that the right of water passage <note>original: "(13)"</note> does not come into the action for the division of common property: for it is either of the land itself; and therefore does not come into the action: or it is separated from the land, yet divided either by measure or by times <note>original: "(14)"</note>. But rights <note>original: "(15)"</note> can exist even not divided by times: as for instance, when he to whom they belonged left several heirs. When this happens, it is consistent that these also come into the arbitration of the division of an inheritance: nor does Pomponius see why <note>original: "(16)"</note> it should come less into the action for the division of common property than that for the division of an inheritance. Therefore, in cases of this kind, it comes into the action for the division of common property [also], so that the aforementioned rights may be divided either by measure or by times <note>original: "(17)"</note>.

Concerning damage which occurred through the fault of a partner.
20. POMPONIUS, Book 13, on Sabinus.
If he with whom you have common land does not respond to a draft <note>original: "(18)"</note>, and for that reason the villa has been demolished by the movement <note>original: "(19)"</note> of the judge, or trees have been cut down, the loss <note>original: "(21)"</note> will be made good to you <note>original: "(20)"</note> in the action for the division of common property. For whatever is lost by the fault of a partner is contained in that action.

Concerning the office of the Judge.
21. ULPIANUS, Book 30, on Sabinus.
It is fitting for a judge in dividing estates to follow what is most useful <note>original: "(22)"</note> for all, or what the litigants prefer.

If anyone builds in his own name and that of his neighbor.
22. POMPONIUS, Book 33, on Sabinus.
If <note>original: "(23)"</note> I build a wall in my own name and that of my neighbor, whether I intend to seek back the expense from him for his part, or for the sake of a gift <note>original: "(24)"</note>, the wall will become common.

The horses were Kun, Yan, Hun, Hua, Xu, Ji. The rear chariots arrived at the wilderness of Xiangcheng. The seven sages were all lost and had no one to ask for directions. They happened to meet a young boy tending horses and asked him for directions. He said, "Do you know Jici mountain?" They said, "Yes." "Do you know where Dawei resides?" They said, "Yes." *And rule the subjected world, most brave prince.*

*And the Roman court will not be seen changing masters.*
*Moved by these voices, he finally yielded: they go into the citadel*
*With the obedience of the fathers accompanying; the most grateful spouse*

*They proceed in the middle of the night through the safe city*
*With faces little joyful, although (with the senate rejoicing)*
*They were seeking the empire: although they saw all things safe;*
*That grief of the parent was within their divine minds.*
*The mild image hovers before their pious eyes;*
<margin>* perhaps: moves.</margin>
*It * moves the mind, and deep within each breast*
*Remaining undivided, it fills the pious divine powers with divinity.*
<margin>XI. A happy omen is inferred for Justin and Sophia from the crowing of the cocks.</margin>
*As he touched the threshold of the August court with a sacred foot,*
*All the heights resounded with the crowing of cocks:*
*The birds were the first to sense the completed night,*
*And they sang of the joyful day, and they gave favor*
*With constant applause of their wings, and with a sharp voice.*
<margin>XII. Concerning the guards and the solicitude of the royal house.</margin>
*The guards first, who protect the highest palaces,*
*Wish a happy empire for the masters as they enter,*
*And they wall all the approaches with armed soldiers,*
*Lest any contrary one dare to bring a hostile foot*
*Into the August court (such was the devotion,*
*And the caution of the men, and the skillful solicitude*
*Of the good fathers) For who would attempt to be a hindrance,*
*When God had already said with a holy mouth that the empire*
*Was given to Justin and Sophia? and with a powerful wall*
*He had surrounded it, but with heavenly arms the whole court,*
*Disposing all things, Tiberius, provident, had fortified the citadel,*
*He to whom the greatest care of the master's*
*Utility always was: For the greatest world,*
*Nurturing him as a common benefactor, and from the mother's breast*
*Taking him as a boy, had chosen him from his first years;*

Utinam verò impensae fierent, in libros eximios utilissimosque, qui suo merito in lucem vel revocandi vel promovendi; atque alacriori typothetarum industria, impressa ingenii monumenta, non hic angustiis officinae typographicae, verùm in publico celebriorum locorum mercatu exponerentur. Sic feliciori auspicio, non typographia minus, quam literaria Academiae res convalesceret & invalesceret.

<margin>Aliarum rerum quae Acad. inserviunt dispositio.</margin>
Quin & juvabit incrementum Acad. nostrae, teste sermone exoterico, si praeter spartas optimarum disciplinarum, quae nobis Professoribus sunt demandatae, alia munia injungantur aliis, ut exoticas linguas, Gallicam, Italicam ac similes nonnulli discere, & Gymnasticam exercere possint. Datur in illustri nostro Athenaeo quaedam, ut illa comparentur, occasio, atque in votis est, perficiatur magis magisque.

<margin>Joh. Felde in analys. l. 8. Pol. Arist. c. 3.</margin>
Praestantissimus Philosophorum, *iste*, qui, docente Siberiano anagrammate, *sol erat*, talia inter optimae disciplinae adminicula recenset; & in illum Aristotelis locum, non nemo Politicorum scribit: *reprehendendos esse, qui ab Academiis artem equitandi, pugillatoriam, saltatoriam, rejicere volunt, cum insigne addat ornamentum, & ad sanitatem ac virtutem conferat.*

<margin>Marc. Zver. Boxhorn. & Joh. Henr. Boecler. on Typography.</margin>
This Academy has acquired most elegant typefaces, nor does it yield in any way to the Dutch or others in this respect. For the art of printing <term>calcographia</term> <gloss>copperplate engraving/printing</gloss> becomes the conciliator of knowledge, the monitor of industry; by its benefit, whoever speaks something into the public sphere through printed monuments speaks to everyone, quickly and always. But would that expenses were made for excellent and most useful books, which by their merit ought either to be recalled or promoted into the light; and that by more lively industry of the printers, the printed monuments of wit would not be exposed here within the confines of a printing house, but in the public market of more famous places. Thus, under a more fortunate omen, not only the printing press but also the literary life of the Academy would recover and gain strength.

<margin>The arrangement of other things that serve the Academy.</margin>
Indeed, it will also help the growth of our Academy, as the <term>sermo exotericus</term> <gloss>common/public discourse</gloss> attests, if besides the tasks of the best disciplines, which have been entrusted to us Professors, other duties are enjoined upon others, so that some might learn foreign languages, such as French, Italian, and the like, and practice Gymnastics. In our illustrious Athenaeum, there is some opportunity for these to be acquired, and it is in our prayers that it be perfected more and more.

[Chap. XI.] Now the princes of the people dwelt in Jerusalem: the rest of the common people cast lots that they might take one part out of ten who would dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts in the other cities. And the people blessed all the men who offered themselves of their own will to dwell in Jerusalem. These are therefore the princes of the province, who dwelt in Jerusalem, and in the cities of Juda. Each one dwelt in his possession, in his cities, Israel, the priests, the Levites, the Nathinæi, and the sons of the servants of Solomon.

And in Jerusalem dwelt from the sons of Juda and from the sons of Benjamin: from the sons of Juda, Athaia son of Aziam, son of Zacharias, son of Amarias, son of Saphatia, son of Malaleel: from the sons of Phares, son of Baruch, son of Colhoza, son of Azia, son of Adaia, son of Joiarib, son of Zacharias, son of Silonitis; all these sons of Phares, who dwelt in Jerusalem, were four hundred sixty-eight valiant men.

And these are the sons of Benjamin; Sellum son of Mosollam, son of Joel, son of Phadaia, son of Colaia, son of Masia, son of Etheel, son of Isaia, and after him Gebbai. Sellai, nine hundred twenty-eight, and Joel son of Zechri their overseer, and Judas son of Senua over the city second in command.

And of the priests. Idaia son of Joarin, Jachin, Saria son of Helcia, son of Mosollam, son of Sadoc, son of Moraioth, son of Ahitut, prince of the house of God, and their brothers doing the work of the temple, eight hundred twenty-two.

And Adaia son of Jeroam, son of Phelelia, son of Amsi, son of Zacharias, son of Phesur, son of Melchia, and his brothers, princes of the fathers: two hundred forty-two. And Amassai son of Azreel, son of Ahazi, son of Mosollamoth, son of Emmer, and their brothers very mighty: one hundred twenty-eight, and their overseer Zabdiel son of the mighty ones.

And of the Levites, Sebenia son of Asub, son of Azaricam, son of Asabia, son of Boni, and Sabathai and Josabed, over the works that were outside in the house of God, from the princes of the Levites,

And Mathania son of Micha, son of Zebedei, son of Asaph, the prince to praise and to confess in prayer, and Becbecia the second of his brothers, and Abda son of Samua, son of Galal, son of Idithun, all the Levites in the holy city two hundred eighty-four.

And the porters, Accub, Temon, and their brothers, who kept the doors: one hundred seventy-two. And the rest of Israel, the priests and the Levites in all the cities of Juda, each one in his possession.

And the Nathinæi, who dwelt in Ophel, and Siaba, and Gaspha from the Nathinæi. And the overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem, Azzi son of Bani, son of Asabia, son of Mathania, son of Micha. From the sons of Asaph, the singers in the ministry of the house of God. For the command of the king was upon them, and the order in the singers for each day:

<column-break/>

A and Phathalia son of Mesebel, from the sons of Zera son of Juda, at the hand of the king, according to every word of the people, and in houses throughout all their regions.

From the sons of Juda they dwelt in Cariath-Arbe and in its daughters: and in Dibon, and in its daughters, and in Cabseel, and in its villages, and in Jesue, and in Molada, and in Bethphaleth, and in Asersual, and in Bersabee and in its daughters, and in Siceleg, and in Mochona, and in its daughters, and in Remmon, and in Saraa, and in Jerimuth, Zanoo, Odollam, and in their villages, Lachis and its regions, and Azeca, and its daughters. And they remained in Bersabee even to the valley of Ennom.

The sons of Benjamin, from Geba, Mechmas and Aia, and Beth-El, and its daughters: Anathoth, Nob, Anania, Asor, Rama, Gethaim, Adid, Seboim, and Neballat, Lod, and Ono the valley of craftsmen. And of the Levites, the portions of Juda and Benjamin.

[Chap. XII.] Now these are the priests and the Levites, and who went up with Zorobabel son of Salathiel, and Josue: Sara, Jeremias, Ezra, Amaria, Melluch, Atus, Sechenias, Reum, Merimuth, Addo, Genthon, Abia, Miamin, Madia, Belga, Semeia, and Joiarib, Idaia, Sellum, Amoc, Helcia, Idaia. These are the princes of the priests, and their brothers, in the days of Josue.

Furthermore the Levites, Jesua, Bennui, Cedmiel, Sarabia, Juda, Mathania, over the hymns, they and their brothers, and Becbecia and Anni, and their brothers, each one in his office. Now Jesue begot Joiacim, and Joiacim begot Eliasib, and Eliasib begot Joiada, and Joiada begot Jonathan, and Jonathan begot Jeddoa.

In the days of Joiacim there were priests and princes of the families. And to serve in the cavalry, which wages war on hares,
Or in the infantry, which bears arms against birds,
To know no other equipment but the scythe and the sickle,
And no other newspapers, except household accounts! . . .

Above Soplicowo the sun rose and already fell
Upon the thatch and crept into the barn through the gaps;
And over the dark green, fresh, fragrant hay,
From which the youth had made themselves a bed,
Gold, flickering ribbons dissolved
From the hole in the black thatch, like ribbons from a braid;
And the sun teases the lips of the sleepy with a ray of morning,
Like a girl waking her lover with an ear of wheat.
Already sparrows jumping, began to chirp under the thatch;
Already the gander honked thrice, and after it like an echo,
Ducks and turkeys replied in a chorus,
And the lowing of cattle going to the field is heard.

The youth rose. Tadeusz still lies sleepy:
For he also fell asleep the latest; from yesterday's supper
He returned so restless that at the crowing of the cocks
He had not yet closed his eyes, and on his bed
He twisted so that he sank into the hay as if into water,
And slept soundly: until a cold wind blew into his eyes,
When the creaking barn doors were opened with a crash,
The Bernardine, Father Robak, entered with a knotted belt,
Calling out <term>Surge puer</term> <gloss>get up, boy</gloss>, and swinging the belt with cucumbers <note>a humorous reference to the friar's humble, food-laden belt</note> over his shoulders in a coarse manner.

Already in the courtyard hunting cries are heard;
They lead out the horses, they harness the carriages,
The courtyard can barely hold such a throng.
Horns sounded, the kennels were opened;
The greyhounds play, having rushed out happily whimpering;
Seeing the steeds of the hunters and the leash-holders,
The dogs race like madmen at a gallop around the courtyard;
Then they run and place their necks into the collars:
All this bodes very good hunting.

Plot reconstruction:

(i) An unidentified character ‘A’ expresses criticism about the glib and interfering teacher Phanias. (ii) ‘A’ thinks that Phanias should be content with what he already has(?). For he will never be the same as those to whom ‘A’ belongs — despite his wealth(?). (iii) Phanias is very anxious about a group of persons. (iv) He is more than happy, when he hears that (v) Parmenon has seen them. (vi) As far as Parmenon knows, they are safe and sound. (vii) The reason for Phanias’ anxiety was a delay, presumably of a ship’s arrival. — The subsequent points are more conjectural: (viii) The ship went to Crete and was detained there(?). There it was considered to be the enemy’s(?). (ix) This forced the passengers to take refuge(?) with a *xenos*. (x) After a betrayal(? by the *xenos*?) they had to flee(?). (xi) A passenger on the same ship helped them(?) and made them return safely(?) to the place where the action takes place(?).

Possible connections with the *Kitharistes*: (iii) and (vii) would go nicely together with *Kith.* 44 ff., where the lyre-player Phanias expresses his anxiety about his wife and his daughter who had left Ephesos before him, but have not yet arrived in Athens (or are staying in a place unknown to him). Parmenon’s qualified answer (vi) could obliquely refer to the fact that Phanias’ daughter is pregnant, whether Parmenon already knows this or not (dramatic irony). (Moschion, the son of Phanias’ neighbour, had raped her on the occasion of a festival for Artemis in Ephesos: *Kith.* 92 ff.) The detention in Crete (ix) could account for the late arrival of Phanias’ relatives. As for (xi), it is noteworthy that Phanias’ family has possibly returned to Athens on the same ship as Moschion (so Webster, *Introduction to Menander* (Manchester 1974) 157; differently Arnott, *ZPE* 31 (1978) 27, on the basis of the very lacunose ll. 1–27; but even if Arnott is right about κατέλινες (*Kith.* 10), it is not at all clear at what point Moschion ‘deserted’ Phanias’ daughter and whether he has ‘returned’ to her, i.e. wants to marry her (again)). Later in the play, Moschion (or a slave who accompanied him) may then have emphasized his role in ‘rescuing’ the women, in order to make Phanias more favourable to the idea of marrying his daughter to Moschion.

Possible objections to the attribution: (*a*) The plot connections are not very strong and partly dependent on hypothetical reconstructions. (*b*) The name Phanias is known from other sources. (*c*) Nothing in the extant fragments of *Kitharistes* points to Phanias as being a teacher (but see next paragraph).

If the attribution to *Kitharistes* is correct, the critical character ‘A’ may be identical with the speaker in *Kith.* fr. 5 and especially fr. 6 where he seems to question Phanias’ skills as a lyre-player (therefore διδάσκαλος sarcastically?).

R. NÜNLIST

### Wennu
<column-break/>
Master Xu of Hejian was teaching in Enla. When he returned home, he met an old man who scrutinized him and said, "Master Xu, your house is empty of books <note>original: 徹帳</note>. Where will you be teaching next year?" Master Xu smiled and replied, "The same as before." The old man said, "My nephew's surname is Shi; he has been seeking a brilliant teacher and entrusted me to come here to Dongtun to hire Lü Zilian, but he has already accepted a fee from Ji..."
<column-break/>
<note>According to historical records, the "Dashhen" mentioned, whose name was Jin, was a native of Jishui, Jiangxi. He was a successful candidate in the Hongwu era. During the reign of the Wen Emperor, along with Fang Xiaoru, Zhou Shixiu, Wang Gen, Wu Pu, and Hu Guang, he refused to serve the new regime and died for his principles. Later, the Emperor sent someone to observe Hu Guang's reaction, seeing him asking his family if they had fed the pigs, showing his intent was not on death. He wore the clothes of the Fang Xiaoru faction in the marketplace. Shixiu died for his cause... and he wept endlessly. His entire family was killed, while others broke their promises. Details are in the History of the Ming.</note>

Thus the Messenger commanded,
That everyone who died and made that descent,
He has regret for the transition and death,
But it is a regret for the lack of fulfillment.
Whoever dies, he has a body,
Which was the destination of his movement before this.
If he were wicked, he wishes he had been less so;
And if he were pious, he wishes he had reached the house sooner.
That unhappy one says, "I have been,
Moment by moment I have been adding to the veil."
"If I had taken the order earlier,"
"This veil of mine would have been less."
From greed, there is little contentment,
And from fear, there is little humility in that face.
Likewise, from greed, there is little in the mountain,
And from Iblis, there is good prostration in the face.
Do not pluck the feather that adorns the paradise,
Do not pluck the veil that measures.
When he heard this advice and realized the gratitude,
After that, he began to cry in a new way.
Lamentation and crying from the pain-stricken,
Whoever was there was thrown into his crying.
And the one who was asking about plucking the feather,
Became without answer, ashamed, and mourning.
"Why did I foolishly ask him?"
"He is full of his own grief, in a state of agitation."
Water dripped from his wet eyes,
In every drop, a hundred answers were contained.
Crying with sincerity strikes the soul,
Until it makes the heavens and the throne cry.
The intellect and the hearts that are of the Throne,
Are in a veil, striking from the light of the Throne.

### On the explanation that the intellect and the spirit are imprisoned in water and clay like Harut and Marut in the well of Babel

Like Harut and Marut, those two pure ones,
They are bound here in a fearsome well.
The world of intellect and appetite is within,
Within this well, until they are bound by the crime.
Magic and anti-magic, without choice,
From these two, the good and the wicked learn.
But take that bad advice as a guide,
Do not learn magic, and do not collect it.
"We teach magic," says the other,
"For the sake of trial and examination."
"Condition is required for the test,"
"You have no choice without power."
Desires are like sleeping dogs,
Within them, good and evil are hidden.
Since there is no power, these ten have slept,
Like a name on a foot or a body.
Until a carrion comes in between,
The mystery of the images of greed, what was it in the mine?
When a carrion donkey died in that alley,
A hundred sleeping dogs were awakened by it.
Greeds went into the treasure of the unseen,
Bringing an attack and striking at the pocket.

quid habeat iucundum circa se & voluptariu. Quædam remedia aliis partibus corporis salutaria, velut fœda & indecora, adhibere aliis nequeunt: & quod alibi prodesset fine damno verecundiæ, id fit inhonestū loco vulneris. Non te pudet luctū voluptate sanare? Seuerius ista fananda est. Illud potiùs admone, nullum mali sensum ad eum qui perit, peruenire. Nam si peruenit, non periit. Nulla, inquam, eū res lædit, qui nullus est. Vivit, si læditur. Vtrū putas illi malè esse, quod nullus est, an quod est adhuc aliquis? Atqui nec ex eo potest ei tormentū esse, quod non est; quis enim nullius sensus est? nec ex eo, quod est. Effugit enim maximum mortis incommodum no esse. Illud quoque dicamus ei qui deflet ac desiderat in ætate prima raptum: Omnes quantum ad breuitatem æui, si vniuerso compares, & iuuenes & senes in æquo sumus. Minus enim ad nos ex omni ætate venit, quàm quod minimum esse quis dixerit: quoniam quidem minimum aliqua pars est. Hoc quod viuimus, proximū nihilo est: & tamen ob dementiam nostrā latè disponitur. Hæc tibi scripsi, non tanquam expectaturus esses remediū à me tam ferū. liquet enim mihi te locutū tecū, quicquid lecturus es: sed vt castigaré illam exiguam moram, qua à te recessisti & in reliquū exhortarer, cōtra fortunā tolleres animos, & omnia eius tela, nū tanquā possent venire, sed tanquām vtique essent ventura, prospiceres.

EP. C. FABIANI Papirii libros, qui inscribūtur Ciniliū, legisse te cupidissimè scribis, sed nō respondisse expectationi tuæ. Deinde, oblitus de philosophagi compositionem eius accusas. Puta esse quod dicis: & effundi verba non fingi. Primum habet ista res suam gratiam: & est decor proprius orationis leniter lapsæ. Multum enim interest existimo vtrum exciderit, an fluxerit. Nunc in hoc quoque quod dicturus sum, ingens differentia est. Fabianus mihi non effundere videtur orationem, sed fundere, adeo larga est, & sine perturbatione, non fine cursu tamen, veniens. illud planè fatetur & præfert, non esse se tractatam, nec diu tortam, sed ita vt eius esse credamus. Mores ille, non verba composuit: & animis scripsit ista, non auribus. Præterea ipso dicēte non vacasset tibi partes intueri: adeo te summa rapuisset, & ferè quæ impetu placent, minus præstát ad manum relata. Sed illud quoque multum est, primo aspectu oculos occupasse, etiam si contemplatio diligens inuentura est, quod arguat. Si me interrogas, maior ille est qui iudiciū abstulit, quàm qui meruit. Et scio hunc tutioré esse: scio audacius sibi de futuro promittere. Oratio follicita philosophum non decet. Vbi tandé erit fortis & constans, vbi periculum sui faciet, qui timet verba? Fabianus non erat negligens in oratione, sed securus. Itaque nihil inuenies sordidum. Electa verba sunt, non captata, nec huius fæculi more contra naturam suam posita & inuersa, splendida tamen: quamuis sumantur è medio: sensus honestos & magnificos habent, non coactos in sententiam, sed altius ductos. V'debimus, quid parum structū, quid non huius recentis polituræ. Cú circumspexeris omnia, nullas videbis angustias. Defit fanè varietas marmorum: & concifura aquarum cubiculis interfluentium, & pauperis cella, & quicquid aliad luxuria, non conten-

pleasant and voluptuous about it. Some remedies beneficial to other parts of the body cannot be applied to others, as they are foul and indecorous, and what would benefit elsewhere without loss of modesty becomes dishonest at the site of a wound. Does it not shame you to heal mourning with pleasure? Such things must be healed more severely. Rather, advise yourself of this: that no sense of evil reaches him who perishes. For if it reaches him, he has not perished. Nothing, I say, harms him who is nothing. He lives, if he is harmed. Do you think it is bad for him because he is nothing, or because he is still something? But yet, there cannot be torment for him from the fact that he is not; for who is of no sense? Nor from the fact that he is. For he escapes the greatest disadvantage of death, which is not to be. Let us also say to him who laments and longs for one snatched away in the first age: We are all, as far as the brevity of time is concerned, if you compare it to the universe, both young and old, on an equal footing. For less comes to us from all of time than what one would call the least; since, indeed, the least is some part. This that we live is closest to nothing; and yet, because of our madness, it is arranged widely. I have written these things to you, not as if you were expecting a remedy from me so fierce—for it is clear to me that you have spoken with yourself whatever you are about to read—but so that I might chastise that slight delay by which you retreated from yourself and, for the remainder, might exhort you that you would lift your spirits against fortune and foresee all its weapons, not as if they could come, but as if they were certainly going to come.

EP. 100. You write that you have read the books of Fabianus Papirius, which are titled "Cinilium," most eagerly, but that they did not answer to your expectation. Then, forgetting that they are a composition of philosophy, you accuse their structure. Suppose it is as you say: and that words are poured out, not fashioned. First, that matter has its own grace; and there is a propriety proper to speech that has slipped along gently. For I think it makes a great difference whether it has fallen out or has flowed. Now, in this too, which I am about to say, there is a huge difference. Fabianus does not seem to me to pour out speech, but to dispense it; so large is it, and coming without perturbation, though not without speed. That, he plainly confesses and puts forward, that it was not labored over, nor long twisted, but so that we might believe it to be of him. He composed his character, not his words; and he wrote those things for the mind, not for the ears. Besides, when he was speaking, you would not have had the leisure to observe the parts; so much would the sum have carried you away, and things that please by their impetus are almost less effective when brought back to hand. But that too is much, to have occupied the eyes at the first aspect, even if diligent contemplation is going to find something to argue against. If you ask me, he is greater who has carried off the judgment than he who has merited it. And I know that the latter is safer; I know that he promises more boldly to himself about the future. Anxious speech does not befit a philosopher. Where, in the end, will he be strong and constant, where will he put himself to the test, who fears words? Fabianus was not negligent in speech, but secure. Therefore, you will find nothing sordid. The words are chosen, not hunted for, nor, in the manner of this age, placed and inverted against their own nature, yet they are splendid; although they are taken from the middle; they have honest and magnificent senses, not forced into a sentence, but drawn from deeper down. We will see what is little structured, what is not of this recent polish. When you have looked around at everything, you will see no narrowness. The windings of the earth, thus the splendid temples are seen,
Where the city named from the snowy mountain lies.
Rightly does the Mount of Anne and the Mount of Mary yield to you,
Freiberg itself and the Valley give you glory.
*c* The abundant supply of your vein overcame all things,
When your Mountain was in honor at the first.
The sword-bearing Elector, that Johannes Georgius the Second,
The pillar and safeguard of the Saxon House,
Considers calling his spirit back from troublesome cares,
And of his own accord to enter the houses of the Snowy Mountain,
Leaving Dresden <note>d</note> accompanied by a troop of horsemen
*e* He comes here, and with the pomp which is usual for Dukes.
The knights precede in order with radiant arms,
The clear trumpets give forth sound with a warning voice.

*a* Albinus' Chronicle, title 14, folio 184.
*b* Miners are called "Ants". Albinus' Mining Chronicle, title 6, folio 56.
*c* Albinus' Mining Chronicle, title 4, folio 35.
*d* July 19.
*e* July 21, His Electoral Serene Highness entered Schneeberg.

For in Asia, most places are ruled by kings. And where men are not masters of themselves, nor autonomous, but are ruled by others, it is not their concern to practice for war, but rather how they might not appear warlike. For the risks are not the same. It is likely that they must campaign, toil, and die by necessity for their masters, even when separated from their children, their wives, and the rest of their friends. And whatever good and brave deeds they perform, their masters grow and increase from them, while they themselves reap the risks and deaths. Moreover, with such men, it is necessary that the land becomes deserted due to being unwarlike and slothful. So that even if one is naturally brave and stout-hearted, his mind is turned away by the laws. A great proof of these things is this: those in Asia, whether Greek or barbarian, who are not ruled by masters but are autonomous and toil for themselves, these are the most warlike of all. For they risk the dangers for themselves, and they themselves carry off the prizes of courage, and likewise the punishment for cowardice. 10. The doubtful ῑ is preceded by a horizontal stroke above the line like those above numerals.

Fr. 3. 1-4. These lines seem to form a connected note on the Μαργιανοί; cf. Strabo xi. 510-1, where the Ἄμαρδοι, Μαργιανοί, and Σκύθαι are mentioned in close connexion; possibly Μαργιανῶν is to be restored in l. 2. ἐνθουσιάζουσι (?) in l. 3 suggests that the name may have been connected with μάργος; cf. Hesych. μαργαίνει, ὑβρίζει, ἐνθουσιά, μαίνεται. Several writers of Σκυθικά are known, e.g. Agathon of Samos (Plutarch, Fluv. iv. 5) and Ctesippus (op. cit. v. 2).

5. There is perhaps just room for Ἀντικλε[ίδη]ς, i. e., presumably, the Athenian historian; the preceding word was possibly δ]ηλοι.

6. Which of the various writers named Asclepiades is meant is not clear. A relative perhaps followed ἐν; a numeral and ἐπιγρα|μμάτων is less likely.

8. Ἡρακ[λείδη]ς: perhaps the author of the Ξένη φωνή mentioned in l. 66, or e.g. Heraclides Lembus, who was probably the compiler of a work on Πολιτεῖαι (cf. Fr. 2. 4, 8, Fr. 3. 21) among other treatises (cf. 1867 int.).

10. κα]τὰ Ἀσιαν: cf. l. 17; but the division ] τα Ασιανα is of course possible.

13. Possibly Διονυσιος] ο Ἰτυκαιος, the writer of a Ῥιζοτομικά who is mentioned by Steph. Byz. s. v. Ἰτύκη.

19. ονομασιων may well be part of the title of some treatise.

27. Παρ]θοι more probably than ο]ρθοι, perhaps.

29-35. ‘μέλισσαι: the priestesses of Demeter. The same Apollonia (?) in the first book (says): “When bringing to the Nymphs the basket together with the loom and the work of Persephone she first went to Paros, and having been entertained in the palace of the king Melissus she presented to his daughters, who were 60 in number, the loom of Persephone, and delivered first to them her sufferings and mysteries; whence the women who took part in the Thesmophoria were thereafter called Melissae”.’

l. 29. A spot of ink in the margin is very doubtfully identified as ϵ, but its position points to a projecting word, so that a new paragraph is indicated. Cf. Hesych. μέλισσαι· αἱ τῆς Δήμητρος μύστιδες, Porphyr. De antr. Nymph. 18 τὰς Δήμητρος ἱερείας ὡς τῆς χθονίας θεᾶς μυστίδας μελίσσας οἱ παλαιοὶ ἐκάλουν, Schol. Pind. Pyth. iv. 106. Though the letters at the beginning of the line are mostly broken, the remains well suit the reading adopted, with which Ἀπολλ[ωνια] or Ἀπολλ[ωνις] seems unavoidable.

30. For the κάλαθος cf. e. g. Callim. H. Cer. 1 sqq., 121 sqq., and Schol. H. Cer. 1 ὁ Φιλάδελφος Πτολεμαῖος κατὰ μίμησιν τῶν Ἀθηναίων ἔθη τινα ἵδρυσεν ἐν Ἀλεξανδρείᾳ, ἐν οἷς καὶ τὴν τοῦ καλάθου πρόοδον. ἔθος γὰρ ἦν ἐν Ἀθήναις ἐν ὡρισμένῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐπὶ ὀχήματος φέρεσθαι κάλαθον ἐς τιμὴν τῆς Δήμητρος. The κάλαθος worn on the head is a common emblem both of Demeter and Persephone. References to the ἱστός of the latter do not seem to occur.

ταις Νυμφαις: cf. Schol. Pindar, Pyth. iv. 106 ὅτι δὲ καὶ τὰς περὶ τὰ ἱερὰ νύμφας μελίσσας ἔλεγον Μνασέας ὁ Παταρεὺς ἀφηγεῖται λέγων . . . ἄνευ γὰρ Νυμφῶν οὔτε Δήμητρος ἱερὸν τιμᾶται . . . οὔτε γάμος οὐδεὶς ἄνευ Νυμφῶν συντελεῖται.

31-2. ᾱ = πρῶτον: l. ξενισθεῖσαν. Melissus king of Paros and his 60 daughters are apparently not elsewhere mentioned. Paros, however, was prominent in the worship of Demeter; cf. e. g. Homer, H. Demet. 491, where Paros is mentioned next to Eleusis, Nicanor, ap. Steph. Byz. s. v. Πάρος, who says that the name Δημητριάς was applied to the island, and the statement in Schol. Aristoph. Av. 1764 that Archilochus wrote a hymn to Demeter at Paros. deposits annually in Ireland, the Hebrides, and Norway seeds of tropical plants (1), and sometimes even barrels of French wine, perfectly preserved, wreckage from ships that were shipwrecked in the Antilles. Barrels filled with palm oil, part of a cargo of English ships shipwrecked at Cape Lopez on the coast of Africa, were recovered in Scotland after they had crossed the Atlantic twice: once from east to west, between the 2nd and 12th degrees of latitude, favored by the equatorial current; another time from west to east, by means of the <term>Gulf-Stream</term>, between the 45th and 55th degrees of latitude. In calm weather, this latter current, coming from Cape Hatteras, terminates under the meridian of the great Sargasso Sea (<term>Fucus natans</term>), which is located slightly to the west of Corvo; but as soon as the westerly winds begin to dominate, or as, due to other meteorological causes, the current raises the water level in the Gulf of Mexico or the Bahama Channel, the islands of Corvo or Flores are enveloped by the <term>Gulf-Stream</term>, which then splits into two branches, one of which heads toward the northeast, and the other toward the south and southeast (2).

History, both ancient and modern, furthermore signals a great number of facts analogous to that of the objects transported to the Azores, and which must have made such a strong impression on the observant mind of Columbus. It is known that Greenlanders were often pushed by currents and northeasterly winds toward the Orkneys; in 1682, one was seen at the southern tip of the island of Eda, who hid from pursuit when people tried to capture him. He turned to think: "A-Bao is perhaps not as beautiful as a heavenly being, why does she hold herself in such high regard?" From then on, <margin>This is an evil custom.</margin> his earlier thoughts grew cold. It happened to be the Qingming Festival. According to custom, women went out on this day, and light-hearted young men also formed groups to follow and observe. A friend from his society forcefully invited him to go. Someone teased him: "Do you not want to see the beauty?" Sun knew it was a joke, but because he had been teased by the girl, he also wanted to see what she was like. He happily followed the crowd to search for her. From afar, he saw a woman resting under a tree.

§. 3. Now in the mutual struggle of words between <term>Romanus</term> and <term>Crusius</term>, let us see which of them inflicted injury upon the other. And first, indeed, this is my opinion: that <term>Crusius</term> proceeded against his adversary throughout the *Astri Eclipse* <note>original: "Astri Eclipsi" - likely a satirical work title</note> with notable moderation, so that as a defender of what is fair and good, he should not be considered to have crossed the limits through the license of calumny. For a person is not presumed to be slandering who retorts against an adversary the insults hurled at him for the purpose of his own defense. This is accepted among legal scholars and theologians; but a defender begins to be guilty of injury when he objects to an adversary with crimes, whether true or false, which do not pertain to the proof and defense of the cause and the law. <term>Panormitanus</term> <note>refers to Nicolaus de Tudeschis</note> in chapter *cum te*, number 29, regarding *Sententia & re Judicata* <gloss>judgment and decided matter</gloss>; <term>Joannes Andreas</term> in his additions to the *Speculum* under the title *de injuriis* <gloss>on injuries</gloss>; <term>Angelus</term> <note>refers to Angelus de Ubaldis</note> in his treatise on *maleficiis* <gloss>crimes</gloss> under the word *verba contumeliosa* <gloss>insulting words</gloss>; <term>Oldradus</term> in council 53; and the Doctors in the final law of the *Digestis* <gloss>Digest</gloss> on *quod quisque juris* <gloss>what everyone of right</gloss>; and <term>Covarrubias</term> in book 1 of *variarum resolutionum* <gloss>various resolutions</gloss>, chapter 11, number 7. Furthermore, one will be held for injuries if he cannot prove the crimes objected to for his own defense, even if it is in the interest of the commonwealth to know them, which <term>Binsfeldius</term> attests is the common opinion in *de injuriis*, chapter 1, question 9, conclusion 6, citing <term>Julius Clarus</term> and others.

§. 4. Furthermore, it is not held among written injuries of the word if someone, while protecting themselves from objected

<column-break/>

crimes, says: "It is false what you say." For these words are used even in law as civil terms, such as "you assert falsely" in the law *falso* regarding various rescripts in the *Codice* <gloss>Code</gloss>; "it is falsely persuaded to you" in the law *falso* regarding the common property of others. Indeed, if someone says to an attacker using injurious words, "You are lying," he is presumed to have done so for the sake of just defense, according to the text in the law *quae omnia* paragraph in the *Digestis* regarding *procuratoribus* <gloss>proxies</gloss>. <term>Bartolus</term> and <term>Angelus</term> are of the same opinion there. And if someone thereafter objects to a slanderer that he is slandering, that has even more excuse, because he is merely repelling an injury with the moderation of blameless protection. This is gathered from the same authors on the aforementioned law and from <term>Castrensis</term> in the final law of the *Digestis* on *quod quisque juris*, number 36; <term>Speculator</term> in the title *de accusationibus* <gloss>on accusations</gloss> at the verse "what if I called you a thief"; <term>Panormitanus</term> in the said chapter *cum te*, number 25. Finally, in mutual injuries, it is worth knowing who first attacked and gave the cause and beginning to the brawl; for he who defends, if he did not exceed the legitimate limits of defense, is not held for the repelled injury, as <term>Tholosanus</term> proves from various laws in Book 38 of his *Syntagmate juris universi* <gloss>Treatise on Universal Law</gloss>, chapter 7. Lastly, as the same author taught in chapter 6, an injury that is committed in writing is to be judged greater, inasmuch as it was done deliberately and persists longer in the sight of men. Wherefore, whoever has written, composed, published, or with malicious intent caused a pamphlet, poem, painting, or history to be made for the infamy of someone, is held by the name of injury, paragraph *injuriâ* of *de injuriis*. In <term>Justinian</term>, the defendant convicted by that name is rendered *intestabilis* <gloss>unable to testify</gloss>; law *lex Cornelia*, paragraph *si quis librum* <gloss>if anyone a book</gloss>, and law *qui* under the title *Senatus Consultum*. A reconstruction of the principal acts in this ritual may be made from the commentary, but it is perforce scanty and deficient by the very nature of our sources. The priests naturally choose only the salient features of the ritual for their explanations, and the acts whose meanings are explained are not chosen in the actual order of their occurrence. That is evident from the small fragment given above. the verse as he had written it before, that is "Although a thousand pens, are tired of it, and already through every valley," which was as much as if he had said throughout the world. Whence, by divine judgment changing it, and leaving it then, as one reads, he came to flee that arrogance, which by chance could have been attributed to him. "Which gain faith for the painful LIFE," that is, they bear witness to how much my miserable life and anxiety is, and coming to the invocation (which is so closed that it is scarcely perceived that it is invoked) he says, "And if here memory does not aid me, let the martyrs excuse it, and let a THOUGHT also excuse it," that is, an amorous one, which gives it anguish, in such a way that it makes every other thought of whatever other thing one might wish flee, and furthermore it makes it forget itself; holding the INSIDE of him, the soul, and he the HUSK, the body. Whence elsewhere: "Po, well may you carry away the husk."

I say; that from the day when the first assault
Love gave me, many years had passed;
So that I was changing my youthful affection:
And around my heart frozen thoughts
Had made an almost adamant enamel,
Which did not allow the hard affection to loosen:
A tear did not yet bathe my breast,
Nor did it break my sleep; and that, which was not in me,
Seemed to me a miracle in others.
Alas, what am I? What was I?
One praises the life at the end, and the day at the evening.
For the cruel one, of whom I speak, feeling
That until then, struck by his arrow,
It had not passed beyond my garment,
Took into his escort a powerful lady;
Toward whom never did much avail, or avails,
Wit, or force, or asking for pardon.
The two transformed me into what I am,
Making me of a living man a green laurel;
Which for the cold season does not lose its leaf.

<column-break/>

HAVING PROPOSED & invoked, he now comes to the narration, and says that from the day that the first assault occurred, intending that which he had when he was fifteen or sixteen years old—not because he had not been in love with other women before M. Laura, because if we want to order it well; rising through the degrees of human life; considering the appetites of each age, we will clearly see that nothing is as pleasing to a small baby as the breasts of its nurse, then an apple, a flower, a little bird, and thus growing little by little, he can scarcely express his voices and words well, and mark the earth with a not-yet-firm foot, before he desires nothing but to play with his peers. Made a little older, he desires a dog, a horse, and similar things, and finally, having arrived at the age, women begin to please him. And this is exactly that first assault, which he says here that Love gave him, to which he shows that he offered resistance until his twenty-second year, in which, conquered then by the extreme and marvelous beauty of M. Laura, he was fiercely inflamed for her. "Many years had passed, / So that I was changing my youthful affection." Many wonder that he says "many years," like those who believe that by adding: "So that I was changing my youthful affection," he began to become old; not noticing that if for only seven years the Trojans went wandering through the world, Virgil gave this addition, "Many," saying: *Multosque per annos / Errabant acti fatis maria omnia circum* <gloss>And for many years they wandered, driven by fates around all the seas</gloss>, Petrarch could have given it even more to nine, which from thirteen to the number of twenty-two ascend, in which he began to change his youthful affection: that is, to grow hairs on his beard, as is customary.

<margin>Axixoca-buizpatlis.</margin> In Recchi exempl. Radix videtur tuberosa, in imo latior, colore flauicante, folia lunata pollices tres cum dimidio, & tres lata.

Pag. 157. Cap. 29.
<margin>Cempoalxochitl.</margin> Tabulosis floribus plantas rariores, atque aspectu iucundiores in nostra 2. part. minus cognitas. Proponimus, alteram simplici flore, alteram multifloram. Polyanthon verò degenerare in magis, & minus dehiscentibus tubulis, ore scilicet magis hiantibus, & barbulis longioribus, alijs verò rotunda, tubuli recifsone sine barbulis; atque domesticas gallinas auidè aliorum congenerum simplici flore folia pluries sine noxa esitasse, obseruauimus.

Pag. 159. Cap. 32.
<margin>Epazotl.</margin> Vera Atriplex latioribus est folijs ferè trigonis, fructu foliaceo, vt aliàs diximus, viribus ferè contrarijs.

The most elegant icon of <term>Piper</term> <gloss>pepper</gloss> thus far, as my colleague noted, was expressed by the most learned Clusius, not only in Exotica, Book 1, chapter 19, but again in the notes to Garzia, chapter 22. But one must also see Christophorus à Costa, chapter 17, regarding pepper, in which he refers to the similarity and difference between the leaves of pepper and <term>Betle</term> <gloss>betel</gloss>, which it happened to us to observe last year through the gift of the most famous Don Pietro della Valle, a Roman nobleman mentioned above; through whose kindness, among other rare exotic things, we received the leaves of pepper and betel. Although these leaves hardly differ from each other in size and cling to trees in a similar way by climbing vine-shoots, they seem to be distinguished not a little in shape and other things. For the leaves of pepper, which are distinguished by not just three but five nerves running lengthwise, almost like plantain leaves, are more fleshy and solid than the leaves of betel; and they approach an oval figure more, ending in a sharp point. The betel leaves, with those same thinner nerves, are much softer and more delicate, and wider around the petiole, and wavy at the top, so that they seem to express the shape of a horn rather than an egg pot. The larger pepper leaf which we had was four inches wide in the middle, and double in length, although some more oblong and even thicker ones are found, yet not as wide at the bottom as in Clusius's picture, but sharper around the petiole, which is not woody but nervous, half the length of the leaf, and has the taste of pepper if rubbed with the teeth. We wished to add an icon expressed from the leaf itself, so that, since certain things were expressed less correctly due to the smallness of the depicted climbing tree plant, the curious reader might look more closely at this larger leaf.

Similitudo Disiuncta est, quando termini quatuor reipsa distinguuntur, ut 1.Pet.1. Qua in re exultatis tristitia paululum nunc (si opus est) in variis tentationibus affecti, ut exploratio fidei vestræ multo pretiosior exploratione auri, quod perit, et tamen per ignem exploratur, comperiatur vobis esse laudi et gloriæ et honori cùm patefiet Iesus Christus. Hic quatuor sunt termini, ut aurum ad ignem, sic Fides ad afflictionem.

Continua similitudo est, quando termini tantum tres ponuntur, sed quorum unus nempe fecundus bis sumitur: ita scilicet ut quemadmodum se habet terminus primus ad secundum, sic se habeat secundus ad tertium, ut apud Ciceronem 3. de legibus. Videtisne magistratus hanc esse vim ut præsit, præscribat recta et utilia et coniuncta cum legibus? Vt enim Magistratibus leges: ita populo præfunt Magistratus. Hic termini sunt tres, Lex, Magistratus, Populus.

Proportio similium inter se est vel ἀνάπαλιν, id est, inuerse, vel ἐναλλάξ, id est, alterne. Proportio ἀνάπαλιν est quando inuertitur ordo aut προτάσεως aut ἀποδόσεως tantum, aut etiam terminorum.
