translation:
Similarity is either Disjoint or Continuous.

Disjoint similarity occurs when four terms are distinguished in reality, as in 1 Peter 1: "In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, that the genuineness of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise, honor, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ." Here there are four terms: as gold is to fire, so is faith to affliction.

Continuous similarity occurs when only three terms are placed, but one of them, namely the middle one, is taken twice: so that, as the first term is to the second, so the second is to the third, as in Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book 3: "Do you see that this is the power of a magistrate, to preside, to prescribe what is right and useful and in accordance with the laws? For as the laws are to the magistrates, so the magistrates are to the people." Here the terms are three: Law, Magistrate, People.

The proportion of similarities to one another is either <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inversely</gloss>, or <term>ἐναλλάξ</term> <gloss>alternately</gloss>. The proportion <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inverse</gloss> is when the order of either the <term>propositio</term> <gloss>major premise</gloss> or the <term>apodosis</term> <gloss>conclusion</gloss> is inverted, or even the terms themselves. Hence the rule of argumentation: If certain things are similar, they will be <term>ἀνάπαλιν</term> <gloss>inversely</gloss> similar; as, if as gold is to fire, so faith is to danger, then as faith is to danger, so is gold to fire.

The proportion <term>ἐναλλάξ</term> <gloss>alternate</gloss> is when the antecedent of a given similarity is compared to the antecedent, and the consequent to the consequent. Hence the rule of argumentation: If certain things are similar, they will be alternately similar; as, if as

# DE PASTORE.

Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; and he makes an antithesis between the hilarity arising from drunkenness and the holy hilarity which arises in the assembly of the pious from pious songs and Psalms. Moreover, when he says "in the heart," the Apostle does not intend that each should sing internally and to himself without the tongue, but he requires a serious affection of the heart.

Therefore, two things ought to be joined in the songs of the pious: a pious affection of the heart, and a tongue that serves to excite the affections. Let these things be said regarding the manner of hilarity.

The time of staying at a feast should not be dragged out to the beginning of madness, but only to the middle of hilarity, especially for a pastor, upon whom others cast their eyes.

Nothing is more foul, or can be said to be so, than for a pastor to drain cups of madness and be the last one to leave home. To me, he who is such a one seems unworthy to have care of goats, let alone the sheep of Christ. By the apostle Jude, such as these are called spots in brotherly feasts, as those who, for pleasure, live in luxury for a day, miserably staining themselves and offering an occasion for spots to others.

Now the situation demands that we prescribe the discipline which the pastor must keep in contracts.

Therefore, first let the pastor beware that he does not seek sordid gain, or, as Paul says, that he not be <term>aischokerdes</term> <gloss>shamefully greedy for gain</gloss>.

Then, that he does not implicate himself in business that does not pertain to him. [He] attempted to declare further the soothing <note>or "consolation"</note> that remains, which is opposed in strength. That this is so will be manifest through the very phrases by which he signifies the changes themselves that have come about for each of the chapters mentioned by parts. And let all that kind be named, for the sake of clear and concise teaching, the "quality of bandaging," being of strength in both compression and the quantity of the bandages; just as they say the name of power is sometimes set in opposition to that of weakness, and sometimes they apply it to the common state of strength and infirmity. Thus they also speak of magnitude and many other partial things in the same way as the general, and now likewise he has used the name of strength. For it is fitting neither to press strongly nor to loosely enclose the affected parts with the bandages, so that the patient does not feel them being placed around; and indeed, one must also accept "the quantity of the bandages" instead of "amount," so that we do not hear of a multitude here that is opposed to fewness. For the...
<margin>differentiation of folding. For this reason, perhaps, he did not attempt to continue, nor to pronounce the terms of the species opposed to strength by division. But that the matter is so, the words themselves testify, by which he shows the very varieties that arise for individual parts as I have enumerated them point by point. But let that whole genus be called, for the sake of clear and concise doctrine, the quality of binding: of strength indeed in compression and the multitude of linens, just as they say the name of fortitude is sometimes established in contrast to the name of weakness; sometimes they use what is common to both strength and infirmity, thus also magnitude and many other things by the common bond of the name. And now the word strength is used in the same way. For it is fitting to bind the affected parts with bandages neither by pressing them vehemently nor by embracing them so lightly that the patient does not feel them being applied. And also, the multitude of linens must be accepted for quantity, so that a multitude is not to be understood by us as opposed to fewness in that region. For the symmetry [provides] the goodness of the binding.</margin>

93 οχεων: with B A J F Z R: ἀχέων b S Stob. Od. 21.302 with same variant. ἀχέων, present participle (intensive of ἔχων) is apparently the correct reading. ἀχέων could be interpreted as (i) genitive plural of ἄχος: but the genitive of definition does not otherwise occur with ἄτη in Homer or Hesiod; cf. Il. 6.356, 24.38 ’Αλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ’ ἄτης (ἀχέων gen. pl. otherwise only at Il. 20.298 μὰψ ἕνεκ’ ἀλλοτρίων ἀχέων, Hom. hymn. Cer. 436 ἀχέων δ’ ἀπεπαύετο θυμός). (ii) = ἀχέων present participle ‘bewail’, ‘lament’, easy enough with μετεστεναχίζετο in 92. But ἀχέων = ἀχεύων is used only with genitive of cause, with internal accusative, or absolutely. If we assume that in the present passage ἀχέων = ἀχεύων is used absolutely and that the accusative depends on μετεστεναχίζετο, we will have difficulties to construe the accusative at Od. 21.302 (at Od. 4.100 πάντας μὲν ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων the accusative depends on ὀδυρόμενος). (iii) = a form of ἰαχέω ‘utter’ (see Buttmann, Lexilogus ii² (Berlin 1860) 103; Richardson and Allen/Halliday on Hom. hymn. Dem. 479). This meaning is unsuitable in both Od. 21.302 and the present passage. Therefore the reading ἀχέων is to be rejected (as by most editors) in favour of ὀχέων, which suits grammar (it is transitive) and sense.
97 θοο. : θοὸν b S J F Z R: θοὸς B A. After θο there is the top of a round letter as ε, θ, ο, and after that just trace at level of the line which does not rule out either of the transmitted readings.
101 . : ἄαται b B A J F Z R: ἄεται S: corrected to ἆται by Heyne. Solmsen compares Hsch. s.v. ἆται. The first trace is of an upright, the second a hook over left, not A.
102 αμωμ[ητοc. No other reading is recorded. μ is largely obliterated, but there is ample space for it, also for ω which seems to show its characteristic connection stroke at bottom into the following letter; that letter, however, has a middle less deep than μ shows elsewhere, and there is unexplained ink beneath its left leg (as though part of the connecting stroke from ω).
103 μαλα: The ink over the second a appears to be an acute accent, but if so, it is misplaced.
106 και [: The first trace just a speck at level of the top-line, compatible with A in the expected καί. The second trace, top of high oblique curving left above the top-line, could be top of ι curving into the vertical.

And to use some example: <term>Crusius</term> cites <term>Baldus</term> in one place with the support of many editions against your one Venetian innovation (which you consider more correct). Immortal God, how often he is whipped! How often is he brought onto the stage as a mutilator, a forger, and a fraud for that same reason! You do this in Allegations 2, 33, 34, 368, 369, 370, 372, etc. Doubtless, to manufacture some number, you count so many errors in these places, not originating from a single little word which <term>Crusius</term> omitted in his citation of <term>Baldus</term> in the law <term>sicut</term> § <term>in Decurionibus</term> ff. <term>quod cuiusque vniuers.</term> And he did not omit it unjustly, since all the older editions of <term>Baldus</term> excluded this negative; indeed, even you yourself in your <term>Astrum</term> <gloss>Star</gloss> quest. 1, n. 38, with your colleague <term>Scioppius</term> in his <term>Astrologia</term> fol. 115, had passed over it, so that you forged the same chain of errors to be cast upon yourself and your friend, which you threw with some unknown mental aberration at the <term>Molossus</term> <gloss>Mastiff</gloss> barking everywhere with the same voice.

§. 5. Now again our man of the <term>Hortus</term> <gloss>Garden</gloss> plows with another's ox, and that too in a foreign field, when he attributes the allegations of other authors to <term>Crusius</term>; thus <term>Crusius</term> is punished for <term>Bartolus</term> and <term>Kebusfus</term>, for <term>Dominicus à S. Geminiano</term>, for the <term>Rota Romana</term>, and others. Allegations 39, 159, 378, and elsewhere. But the miserable reasoner in vain casts his calculations and gathers evening frogs into his bosom. Although this fraud was not of such consequence that <term>Romanus</term> should involve himself by the law of the <term>Rota Romana</term>. Indeed, if I am not mistaken, this <term>Rota</term> of decisions, if used more prudently, would elicit better testimonies of truth from him. He will understand these things more clearly when he has inspected the eclipse of the <term>Astrum</term> with a purer eye.

§. 6. Finally, it is a deed unworthy and most alien not only to any religious man, but even to any honorable Christian, which that Brother <term>Romanus</term>, wandering so often among the Cretans, has marked out against <term>Crusius</term>; for in order to convict him of falsehood, he has admitted as many crimes of falsity as he will be deservedly forced to blush for, once convicted by the public instrument completed at Cologne by <term>Crusius</term>, unless perhaps he has already turned completely pale in his coffin, or has worn away his entire forehead against the gateposts of that <term>Hortus</term>. <term>Crusius</term> produces witnesses, corrupted neither by envy nor favor, jurists of the most perfect reputation, to whose eyes, faith, and public declarations, issued in such number and with such diligence, no prudent person could deny belief, who affirm that the allegations of <term>Crusius</term>, with the places compared with their authors, are sincere and uncorrupted, which you, by badly introducing moles into the <term>Hortus</term> and with secret grasping, have tried in vain to tear down. Is this to sell a deception to the whole world by public proclamation, and to bury the truth with an intolerable disgrace? Now it is finally clear whence so many masks and specters have been raised against <term>Crusius</term> in that prodigious <term>Hortus</term>, as soldiers from the Cadmean furrows. I do not wish to touch upon things conceived elsewhere in this place. The fox is known well enough by its tail. Well, <term>Romanus</term>, though not about <term>Romanus</term>: "Such is the garden as is the gardener," because according to <term>Aristotle</term>, every agent produces its like; according to the idea, genius, and disposition, Alleg. 174, at the end. These few things suffice to overturn the entire mass of that <term>Hortus</term>, and show that Brother <term>Romanus</term> has built in the air. I suppose he wanted to appear as another <term>Semiramis</term>, or I know not what craftsman, who undertook the hanging <term>Horti</term> of <term>Babylon</term> (which signifies confusion) with an admirable work.

<header>OF PELAGIUS.</header>

THE PASSION OF SAINT PELAGIUS, THE MOST PRECIOUS MARTYR, WHO WAS CROWNED BY MARTYRDOM IN CORDOBA IN OUR TIMES.

ARGUMENT CONCERNING THE SAME.

Abdrahemen, the tyrant of Mauritania, following the sect of the Saracens, crossed into Spain and subjected all Christians to punishments or forced them into his sect. When he had taken Corduba, the distinguished city of Spain, he killed the elders of the city or accepted money for them. And when he had imposed such a great sum of money upon a noble citizen, which he could not pay to the tyrant, and was due to be led to prison, his son, moved first by piety, submitted to chains for him. Because of whose beauty, when it had been related to the tyrant, the youth is led from prison; he offers him to the tyrant so that he might yield to his lust. And when the tyrant pressed the youth with many prayers, the youth yields his kisses to the tyrant, the youth seeking with his fist. The tyrant, the youth's embraces refusing, threw him over the wall with a sling and a ballista into the river that washes Corduba. His body, struck by the rocky banks, is collected by fishermen and truncated by the tyrant's satellites. Finally, he is buried most religiously by the citizens.

PREFACE OF HROTSVITHA ON PELAGIUS:

Do not, Pelagius, most brave martyr of Christ,
And good soldier of the King reigning through the ages,
Look with mild piety upon me, Hrotsvitha, a miserable one,
A maid devoted to you with a mind subject to you.
Whom I worship in my mind, and bring forth a song from my breast,
And may it be watered by the dew from above of my small
Breast, the dark cave now, I pray, more mercifully,
So that I may be able to worthily and marvelously record your praises,
And sign your famous triumph with my pen,
And whom you nobly conquered, the world with bloody death,
Having purchased a shining palm with your blood.

The History Follows.

27. PAULUS, book 28 of the Edict.
He who pays what is not owed, thinking he owes it in a certain place, shall recover it in any place: for the same mode of recovery does not follow the belief of the one paying.

If a debtor has paid after being acquitted.
28. THE SAME, book 32 of the Edict.
If a judge has acquitted someone wrongly, and the person acquitted pays of his own accord, he cannot recover it.

Regarding a ward, a madman, and a prodigal.
29. ULPIANUS, book 2 of the Disputations.
Sometimes the person creates room for recovery: for example, if a ward without the authority of his tutor, or a madman, or one to whom his property has been interdicted, has paid: for it is not doubted that in these persons there is generally room for recovery: and if the coins still exist, they will be vindicated: but if they have been consumed, a claim for recovery will have a place.

Regarding one who is both a creditor and a debtor.
30. THE SAME, book 10 of the Disputations.
He who is in turn a creditor and also a debtor, in cases where compensation does not apply, if he pays, does not have a claim for recovery as for an undue payment, but a petition for his own credit.

Regarding an undue promise.
31. THE SAME, book 1 of the Opinions.
He who, by mistake, has provided a guarantee to a creditor for more than the hereditary portion amounts to, has a claim for recovery of an undue promise.

<column-break/>

Regarding an alternate obligation. 1. Regarding a surety. 2. Regarding what a woman gave in the name of a dowry. 3. Regarding an obligation of kind.
32. JULIANUS, book 10 of the Digest.
When he who owes Pamphilus or Stichus has paid both at once, if after he has paid both, either both or one of them ceases to exist in the nature of things, he shall recover nothing: for that which remains will stay in the payment.
§ 1. When a surety makes a pact that money not be sought from him, and through imprudence he pays, he will be able to make a claim for recovery against the stipulator; and therefore the principal debtor remains obligated, but he himself is safe by his own exception: nor does it matter whether the surety or his heir pays: but if the principal debtor should be heir to this surety and pays, he will neither recover it, nor will he be released.
§ 2. If a woman is of the opinion that she is obligated for a dowry, whatever she gives in the name of a dowry she shall not recover: for once the false opinion is removed, there remains the cause of duty, from which a payment made cannot be recovered.
§ 3. He who has promised a man in general is similar to him who owes a man or ten: and therefore, if, when he thought he had promised Stichus, he gave him, he shall have a claim for recovery: but by giving any other one, he will be able to release himself.

<summary>This page covers various legal scenarios regarding the recovery of payments made in error, including payments made by wards, payments by those who are both creditors and debtors, and the nuances of settling alternative obligations like dowries or general promises.</summary>

Peut-être encore seraient-ce les mêmes qui auraient pénétré dans l'intérieur des États-Unis, et commencé ces constructions gigantesques et ces ouvrages de terrassement en forme pyramidale, dont on découvre les ruines sur les bords du Mississipi et de l'Ohio.

Y aurait-il donc eu un âge primordial où les races guerrières ne dominaient pas encore dans le continent américain? S'il exista, il faut le reculer à de longs siècles avant le commencement de notre ère : c'est à cette période qu'il faudrait reporter la tradition d'un sabéisme antique dont il est question dans le *Livre Sacré* (1) et qu'on retrouve longtemps après dans les vallées du Nouveau-Mexique (2). On voit naître presque simultanément ensuite le culte astronomique du soleil et celui du serpent qui répandit alors ses dogmes parmi les tribus indigènes, des sources du Mississipi à celles de l'Orénoque. L'Asie paraît le berceau de cette religion et des institutions sociales qu'elle consacrait : mais on ne sait pas comment elle aurait pénétré en Amérique; car, s'il est possible qu'elle y ait été apportée par quelque peuple émigré de l'ouest, il n'en est pas moins vrai que la plupart des traditions indigènes l'attribuent à des hommes blancs et barbus venus de l'est ou des grandes eaux septentrionales. Ce qui est certain, c'est qu'elle exerça sur les nations antiques de cet hémisphère une action assez puissante pour faire sortir les unes de la barbarie, et modifier les institutions des autres. Dans le nouveau comme dans l'ancien monde, ce fut d'abord sous des formes théocratiques qu'on vit s'organiser la vie sociale. Ces tribus, différentes d'âge et d'importance, mais qui toutes semblent groupées autour des mêmes autels, avaient commencé par s'organiser en monarchies religieuses. Mais en assouplissant l'homme pour le rendre calme et docile, leur culte impérieux avait pu lui ôter de son ressort et de sa vigueur; et comme

Would there then have been a primordial age when the warrior races did not yet dominate the American continent? If it existed, one must push it back many centuries before the beginning of our era: it is to this period that one should attribute the tradition of an ancient Sabaeanism <note>original: "sabéisme," a religion involving the worship of celestial bodies</note> which is discussed in the *Sacred Book* <note>(1)</note> and which one finds long after in the valleys of New Mexico <note>(2)</note>. translation: being asked whether Cato is free, but whether he is among the free. Hence his contempt for dangers and swords. It pleases me, while admiring the invincible constancy of the man not to falter among public ruins, to say: "And his spirited chest luxuriates in muscles." It will be useful not only to say what kind of men good men are accustomed to be, and to deduce their form and lines, but to narrate what kind they were, and to expose that last and strongest wound of Cato, through which the free man lost his soul: the wisdom of Laelius, and his harmony with his Scipio: the remarkable deeds of the other Cato at home and abroad: the wooden beds of Tubero, when they were being prepared for public banquets, and skins instead of coverlets, and earthen vessels for feasts set out before the very cell of Jupiter, what else is this but to consecrate poverty on the Capitol? If I have no other deed of his, by which I might place him among the Catos, do we believe this to be little? That was a censorship, not a dinner. Oh how ignorant are men greedy for glory, as to what it is, or how it should be sought! On that day, the Roman people looked at the furniture of many, and wondered at that of one. The gold and silver of all those was broken, and melted down a thousand times. But the earthen vessels of Tubero will last for all ages. EP. XCVI. YET you are indignant at something, or complaining: and you do not understand that there is nothing of evil in those things, except this one thing, that you are indignant and complaining? If you ask me, I think nothing is miserable for a man, except that he thinks there is something in the nature of things to be feared. I will not bear myself on the day when I cannot bear something. "But I wanted to live, yet to be free from all inconveniences." Such an effeminate voice disgraces a man. You see how I receive this vow of yours. I do it with a great spirit, not just a good one. May neither gods nor goddesses grant that fortune should keep you in delights. Ask yourself, if God were to give you the power, whether you would prefer to live in a market or in a camp. And yet to live, my Lucilius, is to serve as a soldier. Therefore, those who are tossed about, and go up and down through laborious and arduous things, and undertake the most dangerous expeditions, are brave men, and the leaders of the camps. Those whom public peace keeps softly, while others are laboring, are "Turdilli," safe only for the sake of insult. EP. XCVII. YOU are mistaken, my Lucilius, if you think it is a vice of our age, luxury and the neglect of good character, and other things which each man objects to his own times. Nie znać innych, prócz kosy i sierpa rynsztunków,
I innych gazet, oprócz domowych rachunków! . . .

Nad Soplicowem słońce weszło i już padło
Na strzechy i przez szpary w stodołę się wkradło;
I po ciemnozieloném, świeżém, wonném sianie,
Z którego młodzież sobie zrobiła posłanie,
Rozpływały się złote, migające pręgi
Z otworu czarnéj strzechy, jak z warkocza wstęgi;
I słońce usta sennych promykiem poranka
Drażni, jak dziewczę kłosem budzące kochanka.
Już wróble skacząc, świerkać zaczęły pod strzechą;
Już trzykroć gęgnął gąsior, a za nim jak echo,
Odezwały się chórem kaczki i indyki,
I słychać bydła w pole idącego ryki.

Wstała młodzież. Tadeusz jeszcze senny leży:
Bo też najpóźniej zasnął; z wczorajszéj wieczerzy
Wrócił tak niespokojny, że o kurów pianiu
Jeszcze oczu nie zmrużył, a na swém posłaniu
Tak kręcił się, że w siano jak w wodę utonął,
I spał twardo: aż zimny wiatr w oczy mu wionął,
Gdy skrzypiące stodoły drzwi otwarto z trzaskiem,
Bernardyn, ksiądz Robak, wszedł z węzlastym paskiem,
„Surge puer“ 1) wołając, i ponad barkami
Rubasznie wywijając pasek z ogórkami.

Już na dziedzińcu słychać myśliwskie okrzyki;
Wyprowadzają konie, zajeżdżają bryki,
Ledwie dziedziniec taką gromadę ogarnie.
Odezwały się trąby, otworzono psiarnie;
Grają chartów wypadłszy wesoło skowycze;
Widząc rumaki szczwaczów, dojeżdżaczów smycze,
Psy jak szalone cwałem śmigają po dworze;
Potém biegą i kładą szyje na obroże:
Wszystko to bardzo dobre polowanie wróży.

translation:

And to serve in the cavalry, which wages war on hares,
Or in the infantry, which bears arms against birds,
To know no other equipment but the scythe and the sickle,
And no other newspapers, except household accounts! . . .

Above Soplicowo the sun rose and already fell
Upon the thatch and crept into the barn through the gaps;
And over the dark green, fresh, fragrant hay,
From which the youth had made themselves a bed,
Gold, flickering ribbons dissolved
From the hole in the black thatch, like ribbons from a braid;
And the sun teases the lips of the sleepy with a ray of morning,
Like a girl waking her lover with an ear of wheat.
Already sparrows jumping, began to chirp under the thatch;
Already the gander honked thrice, and after it like an echo,
Ducks and turkeys replied in a chorus,
And the lowing of cattle going to the field is heard.

The youth rose. Tadeusz still lies sleepy:
For he also fell asleep the latest; from yesterday's supper
He returned so restless that at the crowing of the cocks
He had not yet closed his eyes, and on his bed
He twisted so that he sank into the hay as if into water,
And slept soundly: until a cold wind blew into his eyes,
When the creaking barn doors were opened with a crash,
The Bernardine, Father Robak, entered with a knotted belt,
Calling out <term>Surge puer</term> <gloss>get up, boy</gloss>, and swinging the belt with cucumbers <note>a humorous reference to the friar's humble, food-laden belt</note> over his shoulders in a coarse manner.

Already in the courtyard hunting cries are heard;
They lead out the horses, they harness the carriages,
The courtyard can barely hold such a throng.
Horns sounded, the kennels were opened;
The greyhounds play, having rushed out happily whimpering;
Seeing the steeds of the hunters and the leash-holders,
The dogs race like madmen at a gallop around the courtyard;
Then they run and place their necks into the collars:
All this bodes very good hunting.

# DE PASTORE.

Psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; and he makes an antithesis between the hilarity arising from drunkenness and the holy hilarity which arises in the assembly of the pious from pious songs and Psalms. Moreover, when he says "in the heart," the Apostle does not intend that each should sing internally and to himself without the tongue, but he requires a serious affection of the heart.

Therefore, two things ought to be joined in the songs of the pious: a pious affection of the heart, and a tongue that serves to excite the affections. Let these things be said regarding the manner of hilarity.

The time of staying at a feast should not be dragged out to the beginning of madness, but only to the middle of hilarity, especially for a pastor, upon whom others cast their eyes.

Nothing is more foul, or can be said to be so, than for a pastor to drain cups of madness and be the last one to leave home. To me, he who is such a one seems unworthy to have care of goats, let alone the sheep of Christ. By the apostle Jude, such as these are called spots in brotherly feasts, as those who, for pleasure, live in luxury for a day, miserably staining themselves and offering an occasion for spots to others.

Now the situation demands that we prescribe the discipline which the pastor must keep in contracts.

Therefore, first let the pastor beware that he does not seek sordid gain, or, as Paul says, that he not be <term>aischokerdes</term> <gloss>shamefully greedy for gain</gloss>.

Then, that he does not implicate himself in business that does not pertain to him. Those who do this are <term>polypragmonas</term> <gloss>meddlesome/busybodies</gloss>, whom even Isocrates condemns, who opposes <term>polypragmosynēn</term> <gloss>meddlesomeness</gloss> to <term>hēsychian</term> <gloss>quietness/tranquility</gloss>, to which Paul urges the Thessalonians

translation: constantly stir the mind of men and do not allow it to be at rest. For these reasons, it seems to me, the Asian race is lacking in courage. And furthermore, because of their laws. For in Asia, most places are ruled by kings. And where men are not masters of themselves, nor autonomous, but are ruled by others, it is not their concern to practice for war, but rather how they might not appear warlike. For the risks are not the same. It is likely that they must campaign, toil, and die by necessity for their masters, even when separated from their children, their wives, and the rest of their friends. And whatever good and brave deeds they perform, their masters grow and increase from them, while they themselves reap the risks and deaths. Moreover, with such men, it is necessary that the land becomes deserted due to being unwarlike and slothful. So that even if one is naturally brave and stout-hearted, his mind is turned away by the laws. A great proof of these things is this: those in Asia, whether Greek or barbarian, who are not ruled by masters but are autonomous and toil for themselves, these are the most warlike of all. For they risk the dangers for themselves, and they themselves carry off the prizes of courage, and likewise the punishment for cowardice. You will also find that the Asians differ among themselves, some being better, others being worse. These changes are caused by the seasons, just as I have said in the previous sections. ### Wennu
<column-break/>
Master Xu of Hejian was teaching in Enla. When he returned home, he met an old man who scrutinized him and said, "Master Xu, your house is empty of books <note>original: 徹帳</note>. Where will you be teaching next year?" Master Xu smiled and replied, "The same as before." The old man said, "My nephew's surname is Shi; he has been seeking a brilliant teacher and entrusted me to come here to Dongtun to hire Lü Zilian, but he has already accepted a fee from Ji..."
<column-break/>
<note>According to historical records, the "Dashhen" mentioned, whose name was Jin, was a native of Jishui, Jiangxi. He was a successful candidate in the Hongwu era. During the reign of the Wen Emperor, along with Fang Xiaoru, Zhou Shixiu, Wang Gen, Wu Pu, and Hu Guang, he refused to serve the new regime and died for his principles. Later, the Emperor sent someone to observe Hu Guang's reaction, seeing him asking his family if they had fed the pigs, showing his intent was not on death. He wore the clothes of the Fang Xiaoru faction in the marketplace. Shixiu died for his cause... and he wept endlessly. His entire family was killed, while others broke their promises. Details are in the History of the Ming.</note>

Day. "Beautiful, it is indeed beautiful, but it is not yet great." Yao asked: "Then how should it be?" Shun said:
<margin>Originally without contrived action to bring about governance, and the myriad things are naturally peaceful. Therefore</margin>
<margin>Sentence structure</margin>
Heaven’s Virtue brings forth peace. The sun and moon shine, and the four seasons proceed. It is like the sun and moon having
<margin>The appearance of movement and chaos</margin>
their cycles. The clouds move and the rain is bestowed. Yao said: "Then is it all stirred up and restless?" The Son
is the union of Heaven. I am the union of humanity. As for Heaven and Earth, they are what the ancients considered great,
and what the Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun collectively praised. Therefore, those of the past who ruled the world,
what did they do? They simply followed Heaven and Earth.
<margin>Wishing to hide his written works in the Zhou archives</margin>
Confucius went west to hide his books in the Zhou archives.

For a father can be compelled if a legitimate cause exists <note>original: "arg. l. nonnunquam 32. ff. de adopt."</note>, such as if he treats his son badly, contrary to piety <note>original: "l. fin. ff. si à parent. quis manum. sit."</note>.
